segments.title: Knowledge and wisdom in historical study
segments.body: Historical study gives people knowledge of past events and an understanding of what happened. Knowledge alone does not guarantee good judgment, while wisdom without knowledge has no foundation in the truth. Analytical training is intended to help students think through what they know and develop wisdom. Historians can only hope that this capacity for judgment is passed on.

evidence.note: The transcript defines the relationship between knowledge, wisdom, truth, and historical study.

segments.summary: Historical study needs both knowledge of past events and the wisdom to judge that knowledge and act on it.
segments.question: Why do historians end up in the knowledge-versus-wisdom debate?
segments.answerShort: Because good decisions require knowledge of past events and the wisdom to analyse what that knowledge means.

segments.title: Technology does not make people wiser
segments.body: Historians are often described as doomed to watch people repeat past mistakes because people may assume that more information and better technology make them smarter. A smartphone now lets one person record a video that 60 or 70 years ago would have required a camera crew and additional equipment. That change brings more capability and knowledge without making the user more intelligent or wise. Technical progress therefore does not prove that present-day judgment has improved.

evidence.note: A smartphone gives one person recording capabilities that required a camera crew and extra equipment 60 or 70 years ago, yet that technical advance does not make its user wiser.

segments.summary: A smartphone can replace the crew and equipment needed for filming 60 or 70 years ago, yet greater technical capability and access to information do not make its user wiser.

segments.title: Historical analysis tests new solutions against past failures
segments.body: Wisdom can grow through experience, reading about the past, and thinking carefully about it. Historical study therefore goes beyond learning facts and figures to analyse why earlier choices worked or failed. People may instead select knowledge from the past to support a preferred argument or course of action. Serious analysis asks whether a proposal is likely to work, especially when new technology depends on methods that have failed many times before. Sellers have little incentive to admit that a new technology cannot solve every problem when buyers may spend billions on it. Historical analysis can therefore inform costly decisions about technology.

evidence.note: The transcript defines historical study as analysis and warns that new technology can repeat failed methods.

segments.summary: Historical study asks why earlier choices worked or failed and whether a proposal built around new technology repeats methods that have already failed.
